history.heading: Chamorro and Carolinian peoples
paragraphs: The Northern Mariana Islands, 14 islands north of Guam in the western Pacific, were settled around 3,500 years ago by the ancestors of the Chamorro. Spain colonised the islands in the late 17th century, forcibly relocating the Chamorro to Guam. Carolinian islanders later settled there.
Spain sold the islands to Germany in 1899, and Japan took control in 1914, developing sugar plantations and bringing in many Japanese settlers.

history.heading: War and American rule
paragraphs: In 1944 US forces captured Saipan and Tinian in fierce battles; many civilians died, some by suicide at Saipan's cliffs. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were launched from Tinian.

After the war the islands were part of the US-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. In 1975 residents voted to become a US commonwealth, which took full effect in 1986, and residents became US citizens.

culture.heading: Island culture
paragraphs: English, Chamorro and Carolinian are official languages. Most people are Catholic, and village fiestas are important. A large share of residents are Filipino and other Asian migrants. Chamorro and Carolinian traditions, such as latte stones, canoe building and navigation, are celebrated.

politics.heading: US Commonwealth
paragraphs: The Northern Mariana Islands is a commonwealth in political union with the United States. It elects a governor and a bicameral legislature and sends a non-voting delegate to the US House of Representatives. Residents cannot vote in presidential elections.

economy.heading: Tourism
paragraphs: Tourism, mainly from South Korea, Japan and China, is the main industry, centred on Saipan. A garment industry boomed in the 1990s and has since disappeared. A casino project on Saipan faced financial troubles. The currency is the US dollar.
